Oppo reportedly cancels Find X10 Ultra thanks to RAMageddon

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (239 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Oppo Find X9 Ultra was my favorite upcoming phone of 2026 but, thanks to RAMageddon, the company is apparently canceling its sequel.
  • Leaker Digital Chat Station reports on Weibo in a slightly cryptic post that, apparently, Oppo has canceled aims to release a Find X10 Ultra.
  • The Oppo Find X9 Ultra packed a top-tier Snapdragon chip and 16GB of RAM, where Oppo’s current Find X10 Pro Max uses a MediaTek flagship instead and 12GB of RAM in most variants, and that one is already very expensive in markets such as Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Oppo Find X9 Ultra was my favorite upcoming phone of 2026 but, thanks to RAMageddon, the company is apparently canceling its sequel.

Leaker Digital Chat Station reports on Weibo in a slightly cryptic post that, apparently, Oppo has canceled aims to release a Find X10 Ultra. The reason isn’t mentioned directly, but RAMageddon is almost certainly the reason. With skyrocketing prices, Ultra phones have been on the chopping block for a lot of Android brands, as specs like 16GB of RAM become harder to sustain at an acceptable price point.

The Oppo Find X9 Ultra packed a top-tier Snapdragon chip and 16GB of RAM, where Oppo’s current Find X10 Pro Max uses a MediaTek flagship instead and 12GB of RAM in most variants, and that one is already very expensive in markets such as Europe.

Find X10 Ultra was expected to offer, in part, a 200MP 1/1.12-inch main sensor with LOFIC, a 200MP periscope telephoto with 1/1.3-inch sensor, a 50MP 10x periscope telephoto, and a 100MP front-facing square sensor camera. In other words, an absolute camera powerhouse, and now it’s dead.

Thanks RAMageddon and AI companies.

Google Messages homepage redesign: Pinned chat avatars, bottom search, corner Gemini

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (328 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In addition to the new app icon, Google Messages for Android is testing a major homepage redesign that has three core components.
  • Revision 11/7: Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.
  • This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s at the moment just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In addition to the new app icon, Google Messages for Android is testing a major homepage redesign that has three core components.

Revision 11/7: Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.

This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s at the moment just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.

You’ll see large contact photos appear above all chats, which pushes the list of other conversations down the page. Like iMessage on iOS, this layout has the downside of not showing any history or last sent information.

Meanwhile, Google is testing another change where search becomes a centered floating action button (FAB) alongside latest chat. When you’re scrolling down the page, you’ll see “Search” in a pill-shaped button, with the other button minimized.

Sources indicate that hate the idea of just the pinned "bobble head" look. I like being able to view message tidbits. Plus, it's directly copying Apple (enough noted). I have to use an iPhone at my job. I hate the pinned bubble conversation look and more importantly it's function.

Otherwise, you’ll see a circular magnifying glass icon and “Start chat” in the pill. The animation that accompanies this change looks nice and feels alive, while boosting one-handed usability.

Google has replaced the Gemini FAB with a button in the top-right corner next to your profile image. This matches the design leveraged by Workspace apps on desktop and mobile.

These updates are currently in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to all testers. Some consumers have all aspects of the redesign, but it appears that Google is rolling out the various components in a piecemeal fashion.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, android tablets have always been a bit of a touchy subject, but it’s abundantly clear that the form factor is making a comeback.
  • Industry observers note that for a while there, Android tablets had hit what felt like a dead end.
  • But, over the past few years, Android tablets have had a renaissance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, android tablets have always been a bit of a touchy subject, but it’s abundantly clear that the form factor is making a comeback. But, as someone who’s a fan of the smaller sizes, are you actually using the gargantuan Android tablets that every company seems obsessed with? In other words – are you the customer for the Android tablets these brands are selling?

Industry observers note that for a while there, Android tablets had hit what felt like a dead end. Bigger smartphones and cooling of the tablet market as a whole, along with the general sentiment that Apple was doing a way better job with the iPad anyway, left the category in a place that felt stagnant – and that’s the nice way of putting it.

But, over the past few years, Android tablets have had a renaissance.

It has been revealed that new form factors, big releases from a variety of brands, and flagship-tier devices left and right. Despite Android’s push into foldables and still-huge displays on nearly every smartphone, tablets are very much back. Prior to RAMageddon’s worst impacts, tablet sales were growing for nearly everyone, and Android brands were seeing a larger slice of the pie.

Sources indicate that anyway, this is on my mind right now because I’ve had a lot of Android tablets arrive in my office in the past few weeks, capping off a lot of tablet announcements in the past few months. I just finished up with Redmagic Astra 2, a tablet I think fits the description of “Android’s iPad Mini OLED,” and I’m in the process of moving into tablets from Lenovo and Amazon. Our Jordan Floyd has also been testing out the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra behind the scenes. And if there’s one trend amongst recent tablet releases, it’s that major tablets seem to be the primary focus among a lot of brands.

Take Amazon’s new Google Play-equipped Alexa Tablet lineup, for example.

The Alexa Tablet 12 is the crown jewel of the lineup, packing the most powerful specs and a premium anti-glare display. It’s the only one that gets a “Pro” moniker, while the 11-inch and 8-inch models are noticeable steps down. Unboxing the Alexa Tablet 8 this week, for example, I was immediately reminded this is not a premium device – the screen makes that clear without any hesitation whatsoever. It was a case of whiplash after setting up the Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 with its 4K display.

It has been revealed that it’s a weird one for me. I’ve never been a substantial fan of these super-sized Android tablets (or iPads, for that matter). I can get behind a 10-inch or 11-inch model, but I find myself more at home on the smaller slates. They’re fantastic for travel as an alternative to draining my phone’s battery, while I find myself just reaching for a laptop instead if I want a bigger screen. A big tablet, regardless of specs, can rarely replace a proper laptop for me, so lugging both around just sounds like more trouble than it’s worth.

Recent findings suggest that but, clearly, people are buying these bigger slates. Samsung appears to be seeing enough success with its mammoth Galaxy Tab S Ultra lineup to keep the 14.6-inch tablet around each year while the smaller sizes are now on an every-other-year cycle. Lenovo’s lineup is virtually all underpowered when the screen size goes down, aside from the Legion Tab that’s now $900.

Are you buying these bigger tablets? What are you using them for?

In a recent development, I imagine that most folks opting for a bigger tablet are using these in the place of a laptop. Thinner and lighter, longer battery life, etc. And in cases like the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro and its $550~ price tag, I get the appeal. Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 takes that down a notch for me at $799 – you’re getting into laptop territory there – but it still is a compelling-enough alternative if it fits your needs. The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra at $1,400 plus a $200 keyboard, yeah I don’t get that one at all.

In a recent development, let’s discuss! I want to know if you’re using an Android tablet, what you’re using it for, and what size you actually prefer.

Ladies and gents, we’ve finally got a upcoming flagship in the US. Motorola Signature 27 is launching on November 19 and looks excellent, though its flashy spec sheet won’t come cheap at $1,599.

Finally, something good came out of Googlebook.

Industry observers note that googlebook is a disaster, but there’s finally one good thing coming out of it in Henry Cavill’s new “Mustache Protocol” game which, supposedly, was built on Googlebook. I’ll bite my tongue there, but the accompanying video brought a needed bit of joy into my week.

I use an 8" Samsung. Not the best in specs, but fine for browsing and reading books. I had a Nexus 10 years ago and gave it to my sister-in-law as I rarely needed something that major. My wife also uses an 8" Samsung, mostly for reading.

Meta’s Horizon+ looks to become Meta VR+ and include 3D movies

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (430 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta Horizon+ is rumored to be changing its name to Meta VR+ and may start including movies in addition to games with the subscription price.
  • Recent findings suggest that meta’s quest (ahem) to distance itself from the Horizon era is in full swing, and the latest rumor indicates it’s time for the company’s Game Pass-like subscription to change its brand name.
  • Recent findings suggest that meta Horizon+ right now includes over 100 games with its $7.99 per month subscription and is similar to Microsoft’s Xbox Game Pass service in many ways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta Horizon+ is rumored to be changing its name to Meta VR+ and may start including movies in addition to games with the subscription price.

Recent findings suggest that meta’s quest (ahem) to distance itself from the Horizon era is in full swing, and the latest rumor indicates it’s time for the company’s Game Pass-like subscription to change its brand name. VR leaker Nori posted a screenshot on X showing a handful of 3D movies coming to the Meta VR Plus service. Considering there is no such Meta VR Plus service right now, the obvious conclusion is that Meta Horizon+ is being renamed once again.

Recent findings suggest that meta Horizon+ right now includes over 100 games with its $7.99 per month subscription and is similar to Microsoft’s Xbox Game Pass service in many ways. Unironically, Meta Horizon+ also includes the basic Xbox Game Pass tier with over 50 Xbox games playable via the Game Pass cloud. Meta offers a 3-month trial with every fresh Meta Quest purchase.

The new Meta VR+ service is purported to include 3D movies as well, although we don’t yet know if this will be included in the regular $7.99 per month rate, or if Meta will be introducing additional content tiers, as services like Netflix, Disney+, Xbox Game Pass, and others do. Based on the screenshot, these will be big-name movies and are likely positioned to enhance the value of the upcoming $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, although all the same content will work on existing Meta Quest 3 units.

In a recent development, meta has been slowly distancing itself from the “Horizon” name ever since the beginning of this year, when its VR division got a major reset. In a February blog post, Samantha Ryan, the VP of Content at Meta’s Reality Labs, spoke about the changes to the manufacturer’s strategy, including the loss of most in-house VR gaming studios. Since then, several prominent VR developers from Meta have gone on to create independent studios, including the super-popular Supernatural exercise app.

Sources indicate that meta then decoupled the unpopular Horizon Metaverse from its headsets, moving it to mobile-only, and has been removing the “Horizon” name from just about everything since then. Meta Horizon+ looks to be the latest significant change, as the manufacturer moves toward “Meta VR” branding, which is clearer and separates its VR division from mobile and smart glasses efforts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-latest lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.
  • It has been revealed that as reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the upcoming Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it.
  • Industry observers note that in this case, Samsung isn’t actually betting next year’s S27 Ultra is going to surpass its predecessor by record numbers; rather, this is all about adding the S27 Pro as a fourth model for consumers to pick from.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-latest lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.

It has been revealed that as reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the upcoming Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it. That leaves the plain Galaxy S27 and the larger S27+ on the outside looking in. In comparison to this year’s launch, the Galaxy S26 Ultra made up about 50 percent of this series’ production volume, for a grand total of 18 million units.

Depends on what the trade-ins are.

Industry observers note that in this case, Samsung isn’t actually betting next year’s S27 Ultra is going to surpass its predecessor by record numbers; rather, this is all about adding the S27 Pro as a fourth model for consumers to pick from. As the name implies, the S27 Pro will arrive packed with features usually kept for the Ultra tier exclusively, including Privacy Display and a matching design, but without an S Pen and with a smaller price. While Samsung prepares to continue holding the Ultra tier at around 18 million units made, the S27 Pro will cut into the brand’s typical 35 million unit total by about 7 or 8 million. In other words, around 20 percent of sales that would’ve went to the regular S27 or S27+ are expected to move upmarket to this more expensive model.

It has been revealed that historical performance implies Samsung is probably correct here. While big displays are typically what consumers are drawn to, it does appear that the S27 Pro won’t be all that much smaller than the S27+. Considering the Pro should slot in right around the typical price point as the Plus model, it’s not hard to imagine plenty of would-be S27+ buyers moving to the Pro.

For what it’s worth, Samsung betting significant on high-end devices usually pays off. We’re on year two of the Fold series seeing big successes — first with the redesigned Fold 7 in 2025, then with the reshaped Fold 8 this year — and the Galaxy S26 Ultra managed to become the best-selling Android phone in Q2 of this year in a list typically populated by iPhones and cheap Galaxy A-series models. Even with prices constantly on the rise, the people yearn for flagship smartphones. You just have to wonder where that ceiling actually is.

Hunter is killing Google Home, Alexa controls for its smart ceiling fans

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.
  • Effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls.
  • Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.

Effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls. Hunter’s app and the included remote will continue to work, but connections to smart home ecosystems will not.

Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.

After this date, Google home and Alexa functionality that relies on this legacy cloud connection will no longer work for HunterSMART fans, including voice commands, scenes, and automations.

This bridge is going away in favor of a Matter connection, with Hunter having been upgrading select models to be Matter-compatible over the past year. But this is only available to “eligible” models, not everyone who was already using Hunter’s existing bridge. A list of compatible models is available on Hunter’s website, with firmware updates rolling out via the HunterSMART app.

Recent findings suggest that some models, such as the one I reviewed a few years ago, require updated hardware. Besides that, the one I have can’t even be re-connected to Wi-Fi to check for an enhancement as Hunter’s Android app consistently crashes during the setup process.

Once the fan has been updated, it won’t be available via the existing link and will instead require re-pairing via your smart home app of choice, whether that’s Google Home or another.

…Hunter is transitioning eligible HunterSMART™ products to Matter, an industry standard designed to support broader smart-home compatibility.

If your fan is eligible for Matter-compatibility, you will be able to continue using all smart functionality within the Google Home and/or Alexa ecosystems after completing the applicable Matter migration & setup.

Once your HunterSMART fan is Matter-enabled, connecting your fan to Google and Alexa will work differently than it does today. Instead of linking your HunterSMART account to Google Home or Alexa, you will need to setup your Matter-enabled fan directly into these compatible ecosystems using the Matter setup available via the Google Home and/or Alexa apps. Matter-enabled devices do not use the legacy cloud linking service for smart controls that is being discontinued.

How can I migrate my HunterSMART fan to Matter?

Depending on your fan model and hardware configuration, a firmware revision or updated hardware components may be required for Matter compatibility. Available Matter upgrade options and instructions will vary by product. You can visit our HunterSMART™ Matter resource page for the latest information about Matter compatibility, available upgrade options, and next steps.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google

Industry News: Googlebook apps built by Googlers add macOS-like status bar shortcuts, keyboard commands

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (542 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the organization’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.
  • In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.
  • According to recent reports, “BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the organization’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

According to recent reports, “BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm.

In a recent development, I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

It has been revealed that the other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.”.

In a recent development, technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Booklight is also on the Play Store.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google.

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.

#384. Tech Report: Why do camera makers partner on phones? I toured ARRI to find out

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1556 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidcentral

Tech Report: Why do camera makers partner on phones? I toured ARRI to find out

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smartphone makers have long turned to the world’s best camera makers to perfect and refine their smartphone cameras.
  • The birth of the iPhone a couple of years later changed the trajectory of the mobile phone industry, with companies forced to focus on building a smartphone.
  • Since that partnership began in 2016, the same year as Motorola and Hasselblad, we’ve seen many of the world’s biggest phone makers follow suit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smartphone makers have long turned to the world’s best camera makers to perfect and refine their smartphone cameras. The trend has grown considerably over the past 10 years, but it dates back more than 20 years to Nokia’s partnership with Zeiss, which began with the legendary Nokia N95 in 2005.

The birth of the iPhone a couple of years later changed the trajectory of the mobile phone industry, with companies forced to focus on building a smartphone. It would take another ten years before the next big partnership began, but Huawei’s partnership with Leica bears fruit to this day.

Since that partnership began in 2016, the same year as Motorola and Hasselblad, we’ve seen many of the world’s biggest phone makers follow suit. From Vivo to Oppo, Xiaomi to Sony, and this year, even Honor, it’s become commonplace to see companies like Hasselblad, ZEISS, Leica, and more all adorn the back of smartphones.

However, is this just a marketing exercise? How much impact can camera makers have on a smartphone camera? Or is this the inevitable direction for smartphone cameras? To learn more about these partnerships – and how they manifest in the latest Honor Magic 9 Pro Max – I flew to LA for a tour of ARRI’s labs to understand more.

Here’s the fascinating history of these partnerships, and why camera makers actually partner with smartphone makers.

The Nokia N95 was the first global partnership between a smartphone maker and a camera manufacturer, and its partnership with ZEISS produced some of the most iconic smartphone cameras in history, ultimately leading to the legendary Nokia Lumia 1020.

Nokia’s ultimate demise in the face of the iPhone then led to a decade-long hiatus, until 2016, when two companies partnered with two camera makers. The irony? Both camera companies still have phone partnerships today, but neither is with the original partner from that year.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Motorola’s partnership with Hasselblad lasted one year and focused on the Hasselblad True Zoom Moto Mod for devices like the Moto Z Play. The other? Huawei and Leica, a partnership that produced some of the best smartphone cameras of that decade and helped birth the modern zoom-toting flagship smartphone camera.

Huawei’s problems with US sanctions cut the partnership short, but Leica didn’t take long to bounce back: the partnership ended on March 31, 2022, and less than two months later, Leica and Xiaomi announced a newly introduced partnership on May 23, 2022. Four years later, Xiaomi and Leica continue to release excellent, distinctive smartphones, including the special-edition Leica-branded Xiaomi 17 Ultra earlier this year.

Sources indicate that not to be outdone, both Oppo and Vivo have turned to camera makers. Oppo’s partnership with Hasselblad started with OnePlus in 2021 and has yielded some of the best smartphone cameras over the past two years, including the new Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, the world’s first phone with three 200MP cameras.

Meanwhile, Vivo’s partnership with Zeiss began a year earlier, in 2020, but it comes with a key difference: the two companies released the partnership with a joint Imaging Lab that has produced some of the most powerful smartphone cameras to date.

According to recent reports, this leads to Honor and the manufacturer declared a partnership with the 109-year-old ARRI earlier this year. The first two phones have both proven unique for different reasons, but why did Honor choose ARRI, and is this just a marketing exercise? My tour of ARRI yielded answers that may surprise you in their refreshing candor.

You probably haven't heard of ARRI, but you've felt the effects of their extremely expensive, extremely precise cameras. Founded in Munich in September 1917, the tech giant has numerous cameras that have made incredible breakthroughs, without which we likely wouldn’t have the smartphone video recording capabilities that we do today.

It has been revealed that the biggest impact has been on filmmaking: ARRI is the filmmaker’s camera of choice for many reasons, not least because each camera is individually tested and precisely made. Every firm claims this, but after seeing ARRI’s labs in LA, I can attest to their precision. Don’t take my word for it; just look at the awards the company has received:.

The latter point is key, but it's even more pronounced over the past 20 years. Of the last 20 Best Picture winners, 17 were shot on ARRI cameras, and you’ve likely heard of many of them, including Oppenheimer, Everything Everywhere All at Once, CODA, Parasite, Argo, and Slumdog Millionaire.

With such pedigree, what prompted the move to smartphone cameras, and how does Honor fit into this?

In a recent development, A lot has changed in ARRI’s 109-year history, but the biggest threat the company likely faces is the generational divide that has coincided with the smartphone. As traditional cameras have fallen by the wayside, the latest generation of consumers likely has no brand affinity for ARRI or other traditional camera makers.

The partnership between Honor and ARRI has the makings of something special. Before this partnership kicked off, Honor had already proven its imaging chops with the Honor Magic 8 Pro last year, but the two devices released with ARRI could yield the biggest jump yet, this time in video.

It has been revealed that the partnership with ARRI focuses purely on video, and the new Magic 9 Pro Max has an ARRI-branded camera mode reminiscent of the organization’s actual cameras. The partnership focuses on color science, accuracy, and quality in video recording, but crucially, ARRI does not make any of the hardware, at least not right now.

Industry observers note that there’s a simple reason: although ARRI cameras have gotten considerably smaller over time, they are still much larger than you can conceivably fit into a smartphone. Further, the company insists on devices meeting the ARRI quality barometer that its customers have come to expect from its cameras. Instead, it turned to the devices customers use most and, in Honor, found what may be the perfect partner.

Flying to LA to meet ARRI, I had one key question: why Honor… and why ARRI?

To find out, I spoke with Stephan Ukas-Bradley, VP of Product Innovation, who has worked at ARRI for over 20 years, and he gave a surprisingly honest, transparent answer: ARRI’s goal is to introduce customers to its moviemaking magic, no matter what device they’re using.

According to recent reports, this reveals up especially well in the first two phones in the partnership. As I discovered, the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max takes excellent photos and videos, but the first device in the partnership is the most unique: the Honor Robot Phone.

The world’s first smartphone equipped with a gimbal stabilizer, the Honor Robot Phone is a videographer’s dream… and a moviemaker’s dream, too. Both phones are videographers’ and moviemakers’ dreams, but the most interesting part is how ARRI’s color science is being used.

Industry observers note that both phones can shoot in LogC3, but what makes them unique is the ability to preview the effect of different LUT profiles directly in-camera, rather than waiting for post-production. Taking it further, ARRI has almost 90 different LUT profiles that can be downloaded from its website and installed on the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, and these are the same LUT profiles used in its actual cameras.

This also offers a unique ARRI benefit: the Magic 9 Pro Max and Robot Phone can dramatically change how you scout movie locations.

Traditionally, a filmmaker needs to hire a cameraman, several production assistants, and camera gear just to scout locations. ARRI’s best cameras can cost almost $100,000, but a smartphone can dramatically reduce these costs and complexities.

The ability to preview LUTs is the biggest unlock for moviemakers; walking around a shoot and filming on the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max with one of the LUTs – or a custom LUT – installed means you have a strong understanding of the final result while you're on site.

Industry observers note that beyond the current partnership, both companies see an opportunity to expand. For Honor, ARRI provides critical insight into color science, processing, and features, starting with video and possibly extending to photography. For ARRI, it lets it introduce the firm to the next generation of moviemakers, especially those focused on social media content creation.

Whichever direction this partnership heads – and as history has taught us, not all partnerships last forever – one thing is clear: ARRI and Honor are a powerful partnership that has already yielded some of the most impressive video recording on a smartphone to date. I can’t wait to see what this leads to in the future. There's a strong chance that Honor and ARRI will make every best smartphone roundup if this partnership continues to bear fruit.

#382. Samsung’s paid Galaxy AI initiative has a giant Gemini problem

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1519 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google

Samsung’s paid Galaxy AI initiative has a giant Gemini problem

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today I’m trying desperately not to buy Sony’s newly introduced nostalgia-bait headphones, reeling from how emotionally invested I was in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (yes, I know I’m late), trying to figure out what a “private, agentic notebook” is, and slowly coming around to the idea of the New York Times owning Letterboxd.
  • Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.
  • Sources indicate that the relationship between Samsung and Google has, over the years, waxed and waned depending on their respective interdependence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good morning. Today I’m trying desperately not to buy Sony’s newly introduced nostalgia-bait headphones, reeling from how emotionally invested I was in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (yes, I know I’m late), trying to figure out what a “private, agentic notebook” is, and slowly coming around to the idea of the New York Times owning Letterboxd.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

Sources indicate that the relationship between Samsung and Google has, over the years, waxed and waned depending on their respective interdependence. Samsung is Android’s physical emissary, powering a plurality of all its handsets globally. But Google, and in particular its services, is the glue that holds Samsung’s smartphone experience together.

The back and forth is over a decade old; back in early 2014, Samsung shipped a refreshed magazine-style skin with its Galaxy tablets that eschewed many of the design tenets Google had been pushing its partners to adhere to. Not only was Samsung willfully defying its most vital partner, but it made a point of barely mentioning Android during its press conferences.

Around the same time, it transitioned its smartwatches from Android Wear to Tizen and began shipping duplicative apps on its devices (many of which persist to this day). The goal was to distance itself from Google as much as possible.

While we don’t know exactly what happened behind closed doors, we saw the outcome quite clearly: Magazine UX lasted one product cycle, and the two companies signed a 10-year cross-license patent deal, which may have helped Samsung prevent any future lawsuits with Apple. Google then sold Motorola to Lenovo, clearing the way for Samsung to continue building its burgeoning hardware business on the back of Google’s mobile ecosystem.

It has been revealed that since then, the two companies have grown even closer. In 2021, they co-confirmed a new Wear OS along with an overarching wearables partnership that has since grown to include Android XR as well. And Google is still the default search engine for Samsung devices, despite reported inroads made by Microsoft in 2023 to convince the Korean giant to switch to a ChatGPT-powered version of Bing Search. (Samsung’s ongoing relationship with Microsoft, which bundles its Office suite on most Galaxy devices, could be seen as a point of leverage for negotiations with Google, too.).

It has been revealed that this brings us to today, and to AI. Samsung was among the first companies to adopt Google’s full suite of Gemini Intelligence products, and its phones often get new AI features before anyone else. But like a decade ago, when Samsung shipped Bixby to kind-of-sort-of compete with Google Assistant, it still wants to offer its own services alongside Google’s.

Recent findings suggest that so a rumor that Samsung may launch a paid Galaxy AI Premium subscription next year for $5/month piqued my interest for the same reason Magazine UX did 12 years ago. Galaxy AI features today are a blend of first-party and third-party capabilities, but none of them are especially useful, particularly when compared to Google’s own Android equivalents powered by Gemini Intelligence. Now Bar and Now Brief, two heavily promoted features in Samsung’s marketing, are wildly disappointing.

It has been revealed that at I/O this past May, Google announced Spark, an agent that goes out and performs actions on your behalf. And while it’s since been somewhat eclipsed by more capable mobile options like Meta’s Muse, it’s obvious that Google is working on a follow-up that will perform functions both on the phone and inside apps.

That’s exactly what Samsung is rumored to be working on with Bixby Action, a spiritual successor to its namesake that, when it debuted, prioritized on-device tasks like turning on Wi-Fi over web-based actions Google Assistant did better.

According to leaks from SamMobile, Galaxy AI Premium will offer agentic upgrades for phone users to “create commands triggers and system routines for daily tasks” or “automate routine daily tasks using Galaxy AI.” Gen Video will reportedly “convert static photos into dynamic video clips,” while a newly introduced Daily Briefing likely does what it states on the tin.

It has been revealed that will Samsung consumers see enough value in this hodgepodge of features paywalled only because they use a surfeit of compute? And what models will power them on the backend?

Right now, Google is in the enviable position of being able to offer its AI at three distinct layers: the model itself, which is invisible to the user; the OS level, which can promulgate Gemini across every Android phone that runs Google services; and the hardware level, where Pixel lets it specialize and optimize.

Industry observers note that samsung, not particularly known for its software prowess, will likely need to step gingerly around Google’s AI shadow while also justifying the cost to shore up its much-needed services revenue. Based on this leaked roadmap, though, I’m not confident it will work out.

It has been revealed that instead, Samsung may want to acquire one of the many up-and-coming AI agent startups whose valuations are rising more quickly than their user bases. While Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have taken up most of the recent conversation, I’ve been using Hark, Town, and Instinct pretty regularly for a month or so and could see them being brought in-house by Samsung and offered either as standalone products or customized for Galaxy devices. As Google is doing with its own AI plans, Samsung could provide Galaxy customers a year of free service, after which they would be expected to pay.

Samsung doesn’t have a great history of building software, but many of its acquisitions, from SmartThings to Viv Labs (which became “next-gen” Bixby) to LoopPay (which became Samsung Pay) to Whisk (which became Samsung Food), have proven successful. Given the current urgent state of mobile AI, I’d forgo the hodgepodge and bring in some outside expertise.

It has been revealed that jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy is the only thing tech media can talk about right now, likely because it has implications far beyond just Nvidia’s stock price. The Nvidia CEO, who is one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech executives, is believed to have been targeted by Chinese intelligence to potentially influence American trade policy around AI.

Alex Kantrowitz’s Significant Technology piece is a useful starting point for why this matters at a global scale:.

Sources indicate that beyond the affair, the real issue is that Huang’s love interest, ex-Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, is someone the United States government believes passed information to the Chinese government while building data centers with Nvidia’s help in Asia. There’s simply no getting away from this detail. This isn’t just an affair, it’s a corporate and national security issue.

Whether Huang can survive the impending investigation by Nvidia’s board remains to be seen, but the CEO has been a stalwart in the tech space for 33 years, and there is no clear successor to his position should he be forced to resign.

Damien reviewed DroidDeck, which I wrote about last week as part of a broader look at Android’s gaming renaissance.

Over the last few days, things have become even more preposterous: the Ocarina of Time remake, which was released on Thursday, has already been recompiled to run natively on Android (though it runs better on PC), largely with the help of frontier AI models.

All of these AI-powered shenanigans come after Anthropic said it would stop making it possible to recreate copies of games, claiming that “recreating someone else’s specific game using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.” Good thing there are no other models capable of doing the same thing.

I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. The last time we saw anything close to this was really the, you know, advent of CGI and digital composites in the early ’90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.

—David Ellison, Skydance CEO, when asked about how AI could impact the movie-making process.

The publication noticed a newly introduced Chromium commit, stating that it's working on adding "Safe Browsing protections" for Incognito mode. Essentially, this would bring real-time protections to owners while they're browsing. This is no different from operating Chrome without Incognito active.

The publication pointed out something interesting: while Incognito mode doesn't (presently) offer real-time protections, the browser will "fall back" on its knowledge of dangerous sites stored "locally." But that's as far as its protections go, and in this day and age, it's not good enough.

In a recent development, additionally, while this is a good thing, the point of Incognito mode is to remain private in your browsing (many aspects don't get logged in your browser). The publication notes that developers are staying aware of this. Developers are working to ensure that privacy-related details about your Incognito session don't leave your device.

There's much for Google to do; however, according to the Chromium commit, it looks like Incognito will benefit from Standard and Enhanced browsing protections—it'll be the user's choice.

Industry observers note that as we've remarked before, Incognito Mode is supposed to be your gateway to more private browsing. But that wasn't always the case. Google admitted to tracking users while they had the feature active. In 2024, Google settled a class-action lawsuit for $5 billion. The lawsuit alleged that the company "misled users" into thinking they were privately browsing, meaning tracking wasn't involved.

Google's disclaimer remarked that it wouldn't save a user's browsing data; however, others (ISPs and websites) could still see it. That disclaimer has since been updated. The tech giant now states the browser isn't tracking you, but Google still can. This didn't sit well with owners, as you'd imagine. Shortly after, Google said it would delete all of the data it captured about users who had Incognito mode active. This was part of the settlement.

Following the preview at the end of last month, Google is now bringing its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model to the Gemini app.

According to recent reports, to showcase performance on larger, more complex projects, Google Antigravity is previewing /swarm. This turns a “single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time.”.

Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.

For legal, finance, and enterprise work, Carbon is said to bring “higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis.” This includes how the model will follow “strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.”.

Recent findings suggest that existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agents (MKA) benchmark. Carbon ranks #1 while using 3X fewer tokens than the next best model across 200 tasks that test a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows.

Other domain highlights include:.

The introductory pricing for Carbon is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30. Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in my role as TechRadar's Senior Fitness and Wearables Editor, I test a lot of smartwatches and fitness trackers. I've tested around a dozen wrist-based fitness trackers this year alone, and what I haven't tested, I've asked other writers to put through their paces for me.

My personal testing bank this year includes the following:.

The devices that other writers have tested on my behalf include the Garmin Forerunner 70, Samsung Galaxy Watch 9, Amazfit Active 3 Premium, Coros Nomad, Suunto Race 3s, Huawei Band 11 and many more. Then there are the items from previous years, as well as devices such as heart rate monitors and smart rings. Over the years, I've tested a lot of smartwatches and fitness tech, and I'm well placed to advise on which Black Friday smartwatch deals to consider.

So, some readers might be surprised when I say that my advice to the majority is to give most of the above trackers a wide berth on Black Friday, with the possible exception of the Google Fitbit Air and Garmin Cirqa.

Most smartwatches, like smartphones, work on churn: every one to two years, a company will release a newer model of the same watch, with a few latest features and perhaps a minor tweak to the design. It's keeps their watch lines up to date, delivering the best-in-class health metrics for buyers, while ensuring that the range regularly stays level with the competition, rather than becoming outdated and requiring a total overhaul. Technology moves rapidly.

In a recent development, for example, this year saw Apple deliver new Siri AI features and a more accurate, redesigned LED sensor array to the Watch, which better detects your heart rate overnight. Wear the Watch overnight and it will give you a Readiness Score the next day, which tells you how much energy you're likely to have in the tank for the day ahead. This can aid in planning your training sessions, and help you tailor your habits to ensure maximum Readiness when you need it.

In a recent development, these features aren't available on the older watches — but previous models do include everything else. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 look and operate the same as the Apple Watch Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra 3, bar a few other quality-of-life fixes, making them an excellent buy on Black Friday. And retailers such as Amazon, Best Buy in the US, and Argos in the UK will be offering significant discounts to clear old stock.

In a recent development, the Garmin Forerunner 170 isn't likely to see much movement in price, but its predecessor, the Garmin Forerunner 165 will see larger discounts. The Forerunner 165 includes the same Elevate V4 heart rate sensing technology embedded in its case, so it's the design, features and software support that are slightly different in the models rather than any accuracy gains.

The same is true of last year's edition of the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra and the Google Pixel Watch 4, both of which were released in 2025: their 2026 successors are iterative updates on these watches. If the price cut is significant on those older models (and it's already the case on the Samsung model below), you should probably buy the older model instead of the newer one.

Recent findings suggest that we loved the device in our Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra review, praising its tough exterior, user interface and its awesome range of features. However, we did note that the screen is the exact same size as the less expensive Galaxy Watch 7’s and we'd have preferred a bigger battery. That mentioned, if you’re an athletic person looking for an Android-based smartwatch, the Galaxy Watch Ultra is one of your best options.

The same is also true of the Garmin Fenix range: the all-newly introduced Garmin Fenix 9 might be super expensive, but the Fenix 8 from 2024 has already dropped significantly in price:.

It has been revealed that save 24% on the stellar Garmin Fenix 8 in its 47mm size. I rated this watch five stars, calling it "rugged, expensive perfection" in my Garmin Fenix 8 review.

Next year, I'm sure I'll be offering the same advice, but with devices replaced by this year's models instead — it's the nature of consumer technology.

If you're interested in getting yourself a latest smartwatch or fitness tracker, look at the previous iteration of a product instead of the latest tech. The cycle of small upgrades rather than giant overhauls means that older tech is still plenty good enough for most people's needs — and it's more wallet-friendly, too.

Of this year's crop of devices, the models I recommend picking up are the Google Fitbit Air and the Garmin Cirqa.

Why? Simply because they're first-generation devices, so there aren't any historic discounts on older models to be found. In addition, they're unlikely to see a refresh for a couple of years at least — certainly not annually, on account of their limited feature set, the nature of screenless trackers, and the fact that they're both fairly high-quality pieces of kit worthy of a space on your wrist.   • Sources indicate that the recent Yandex blog post also appears to blame the small proportion of users who suffered unrecoverable data loss for not making backups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yandex, sometimes called Russia’s Google, has updated its customers in the wake of extensive damage to its data centers in drone strikes. In a blog post this week, the firm’s cloud business boasted that it had “restored access to more than 97% of customer data” [machine translation]. That might sound like a great success, but in the small print, as highlighted by The Register, there’s the admission “the remaining 2.84% cannot be restored due to critical damage to equipment.”.

Data centers operated by Yandex have been under attack from Ukrainian drones for several weeks now. We covered reports about withering online troll activity and online payment system disruption last month. We know of at least three Yandex locations that have been damaged by Ukrainian drone assaults to date.

Sources indicate that the recent Yandex blog post also appears to blame the small proportion of users who suffered unrecoverable data loss for not making backups. When talking about the 2.84% of data that cannot be restored, it notes that was partly due to “the lack of customer backups on the platform.” In contrast, those who made use of the Yandex Cloud backup tools “did not lose any data,” says the firm.

Yandex has now changed the backup policy, so that “at the moment, all virtual machines created in Yandex Cloud work with the backup function enabled by default.” Even if Putin decides to end his war on Ukraine, it might be beneficial to stick with a backup-by-default policy. Consumers are advised to have their own data backup systems in addition to the cloud. Following the 3-2-1 backup strategy, for example.

Yandex is also opening a newly introduced ru-central1-f availability zone at a new location. This is designed to improve the cloud’s fault tolerance and disaster resilience. Servers at ru-central1-f will be more limited in the range of services they can offer, for now. Yandex didn’t share any geographic details of the newly opened datacenter site.

#363. macOS on PC becomes possible again thanks to Apple Silicon translator for x86-64

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (667 w)
Gadgets 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tomshardware

macOS on PC becomes possible again thanks to Apple Silicon translator for x86-64

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the eternal spiral of computing gets yet another loop.
  • Sources indicate that stela is a minty-fresh upcoming project from Tyler Smith, and it's just gotten started, with three releases since the first 0.1 version in barely half a day.
  • The developer answered a couple of questions in the project's Discord server, and he remarked that the macOS image to be used is not modified at all: "Stela provides the translation and hardware behavior underneath that lets macOS go through the exact same restore process you might do on a real Mac.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the eternal spiral of computing gets yet another loop. Apple introduced its own Arm-based chips in 2020, surprising the world with a series of SoCs with a particularly high power-to-watt ratio, a perfect fit for the firm's quality portables. As the designs improved on raw performance, Apple shifted away from Intel-based Macs. That meant that enterprising hackers who ran macOS on their PCs could no longer do so — until today, thanks to the Stela Apple Silicon translation layer.

Sources indicate that stela is a minty-fresh upcoming project from Tyler Smith, and it's just gotten started, with three releases since the first 0.1 version in barely half a day. The author warns that "it is slow and not very stable," but those warnings are somehow invisible to techies trying out a new toy. For practical purposes, Stela is a Linux-based UEFI application for loading macOS 27, presenting a virtual M2 Mac Mini to the operating system.

The developer answered a couple of questions in the project's Discord server, and he remarked that the macOS image to be used is not modified at all: "Stela provides the translation and hardware behavior underneath that lets macOS go through the exact same restore process you might do on a real Mac.".

It has been revealed that the server has seen a substantial influx of people, many of them posting photos of their PCs near-booting macOS. Predictably, most of the questions were about supporting their own particular hardware, but the excitement is palpable.

It has been revealed that to get started, all you need is to download Stela from the release pages, provide a USB stick to then boot your PC with, and, naturally, your own copy of macOS. Stela will take care of translating AArch instructions into x86-64. The translation layer uses a combination of ahead-of-time and just-in-time (JIT) compilation for the CPU, and translates Apple's Metal graphics layer calls to Mesa's NIR instructions.

Recent findings suggest that the hardware requirements are basically potato-level, requiring only an x86-64-v2 — a 2008 Intel Core chip, or a 2011-vintage AMD FX processor. The author mentions that AVX2 and AVX-512 "are used when present," but woe betide you if your processor is that old to begin with. You'll need 8 GB of RAM, UEFI support, a GPT partition or entire drive, and an Nvidia card from the 16xx series to present-day 5000 models.

It has been revealed that there's no Wi-Fi support yet, and Bluetooth is limited, but the list of working Ethernet controllers is extensive, covering models from Intel, Realtek, Broadcom, Aquantia, Atheros, and even USB Ethernet sticks. The author notes that he intends for Stela to eventually support all the hardware the Linux kernel does.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

According to recent reports, purely hypothetically, with AI automation, it's not completely insane to think that much of macOS could be pre-translated to x86-64. Yet such an endeavor has many caveats, namely the fact that a lot of code, like a browser's JIT JavaScript compilation, doesn't exist on the disk image to begin with.

There's also the fact that no matter how efficient a translation layer is, the OS still needs to cryptographically accept it and run it, perhaps requiring further modification still. But we can, in fact, dream of ditching Windows for macOS without being tied to Apple's pricey and barely-repairable hardware.

It has been revealed that it refines sentences, removes filler words like "um" and "uh," and can even understand commands. And now, it looks like Samsung is planning to bring its own version of Rambler to Samsung Keyboard on Galaxy phones.

As spotted by SamMobile, Samsung has started working on a Rambler-like feature for One UI 9.5. The report reveals that the latest internal test build of One UI 9.5 includes a new feature called "Refine voice input" in Samsung Keyboard settings.

The description says the feature can clean up filler words, hesitations, and more, with the refined text appearing once you've finished speaking. The feature is reportedly powered by Galaxy AI within Samsung Keyboard.

Samsung hasn't released any One UI 9.5 beta builds just yet, but once the beta arrives, we expect the feature to become available on Galaxy smartphones that support Galaxy AI. Based on the description, it will presumably work similarly to Google's Rambler, although we'll have to wait to see exactly how it works.

Of course, there are already other ways to access similar AI-powered voice typing features on your Android phone, including Microsoft's SwiftKey and even unofficial apps that bring Gboard's Rambler functionality to other devices.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

It has been revealed that legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

In a recent development, ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

The user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

Recent findings suggest that 9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.

  • Recent findings suggest that the above video documents Muhammad Zulali’s journey from the Jeep failing consecutive smog tests, to managing to hook it up and get readings from the ECU, to tuning and fixing the engine emission issues.
  • This rather old Jeep was failing the California smog tests due to producing too much NOx at certain test speeds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An AI enthusiast managed to get his old 1994 Jeep Cherokee to pass the California smog tests, all thanks to the help of AI and a little electronics wiring skill. This 32-year-old car had only a primitive engine computer, but after connecting it to a laptop via an Arduino Nano board, many settings could be read and eventually controlled.

Recent findings suggest that the above video documents Muhammad Zulali’s journey from the Jeep failing consecutive smog tests, to managing to hook it up and get readings from the ECU, to tuning and fixing the engine emission issues. All the while, Claude provided guidance, and Codex wrote any required code.

This rather old Jeep was failing the California smog tests due to producing too much NOx at certain test speeds. It initially failed at 25mph. Then, after Zulali made some adjustments to the oxygen mix, it failed at both 25mph and 50mph. Yes, it got worse.

Zulali admits he was effectively making adjustments blind, and subsequent regulatory pollution tests cost nearly $100 each time. That’s clearly a major problem, but we have AI to help us in 2026. Actually, it was AI and a $3 microcontroller, contributing to a total bill of materials of no more than $15.

In a recent development, the first hurdle facing the possible AI solution was the question of how to interface an old car and a fresh laptop. Claude told the Jeep owner that the engine communicated on a Chrysler SCI bus at ~7,800 baud, which was electrically inverted compared to a typical serial port. An Arduino Nano can handle the required inversion and hook up the data to a modern computer. The Nano was breadboarded, with a few necessary wires, three of which connected to the 6-pin diagnostic plug in the Cherokee.

The first connection attempt was a success, but only coolant temperature and battery voltage were charted by the system to begin with. Zulali wanted more data points plus some controls to fix the smog test problem. After a couple of red herrings regarding the engine “running rich” with 22% extra fuel, based on other car model data, the Jeep owner got Claude to collect data from test drives. The AI logged engine data and fault codes during a drive at 25 mph and at 50 mph to see what was happening. It was also let loose to control things like fuel pressure.

Sources indicate that with what looked like a credible diagnosis and solution in hand, Zulali wanted to reflash the car’s main ECU with AI-tweaked code that would mean it could pass all the California smog tests. Unfortunately, this car’s computer was just a few months too old to feature reflashable firmware. Instead, the Jeep owner got Codex to inject and run custom code inside a nearby EEPROM.

Sources indicate that “Claude did most of the diagnostic work and Codex did pretty much all of the memory work,” admits Zulali. “I just did the wiring and the driving.” He added that he didn’t need the services of a mechanic or a Chrysler dealer tool for this feat.

In a recent development, in addition to the video, the Cherokee emissions fixer has created a GitHub repository for this project, dubbed xj-scanner. It is free software distributed under the GPLv3 license.

It has been revealed that my MacBook Pro stays at home, running Cursor, the local development servers, and everything else my projects need. With Workbench, I can access that desktop remotely, ask Cursor to make changes, scroll through its summaries with two fingers, review the results, and check the running build in Cursor's built-in browser.

On a Mac or iPad, Workbench feels like a fairly traditional desktop development experience. Its unified display mode resizes your Mac's desktop to fit your remote device's resolution and form factor, aiming to offer a more natural, single-app experience. However, switching between apps isn't particularly straightforward, and navigating the interface can sometimes feel a little jittery.

In a recent development, on the Duo, I generally keep unified display mode disabled, which lets me pinch and zoom into different areas of the remote desktop. It's a surprisingly effective way to navigate a full macOS interface on a smaller screen, particularly when I want to focus on Cursor's chat or inspect a specific part of a project.

It has been revealed that I can also open Chrome to check a locally running website, although I generally find it easier to do everything within Cursor when using the Duo. The workflow is essentially identical to what I was already doing on my iPad; the difference is that I now have access to it on a device that folds into my pocket.

That sounds like a small distinction, but in practice, it's enormous.

Recent findings suggest that the major unlock is being able to leave my Mac at home and check progress on any build, including previewing it, without needing to configure every device with my login credentials, SSH keys, or local codebase. Instead of waiting until I'm settled on a plane or pulling out my iPad Pro and Magic Keyboard, I simply unfold my iPhone Duo and keep coding.

In a recent development, the only problem? It's so convenient that it's taken up even more of my life.

If you've ever tried to use a conventional desktop terminal through a remote desktop app or on a touchscreen, you'll know how frustrating it can be. Tiny text, awkward cursor placement, keyboard shortcuts, and interfaces designed for a mouse and keyboard can make even simple tasks unnecessarily difficult. Add in a Delete key that doesn't always work — a common problem I've encountered across several apps — and text that fails to render properly due to input lag, and even the simplest tasks can swiftly become incredibly frustrating.

That's why a fresh feature recently introduced in Workbench's Duo-optimized app has rapidly become one of my favorite parts of this setup.

Workbench now offers a native terminal interface that lets me interact with the terminal on my Mac remotely, without navigating a traditional macOS Terminal window through the screen viewer. Better still, I can display the terminal alongside the remote desktop in a split-screen layout. It's brilliant.

I can interact with the terminal using an interface optimized for foldables, but with a familiar Terminal design, and then glance across at Cursor or the running build without constantly switching views or changing apps on the remote Mac.

It's a much more natural experience than trying to control a desktop terminal on a folding phone, and it addresses one of the biggest frustrations I've encountered with remote development.

Recent findings suggest that what makes this particularly interesting is how Workbench has embraced the iPhone Duo itself. The team developed a series of experiences optimized for Apple's upcoming form factor, even without a retail sample of the phone to work with.

Recent findings suggest that I originally set up Workbench earlier this year because I wanted to keep my development environment running at home while traveling, particularly when flying. It has been revealed that with my Mac running everything at home, I can use the connection to interact with my development environment instead of relying on it to keep the underlying processes running. The actual work continues on my Mac, whether I'm connected or not.

According to recent reports, over the past week, I've used the Duo to move coding sprints forward, review changes, work through migrations, and have some fairly intense planning discussions with Cursor, including during that flight. The nano-texture folding display is also a pleasure to use, especially when reading through longer summaries or spending extended periods interacting with the remote desktop.

In a recent development, none of these things fundamentally changes how Cursor works or what my Mac can do. They simply remove the friction between having a few spare minutes and actually getting something done.

And that has completely changed how I approach my projects.

Recent findings suggest that there are compromises, of course. The iPhone Duo doesn't offer the same expansive workspace as an iPad or MacBook, and Apple's multitasking features still aren't as flexible as those on Android foldables like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. Sometimes, too, a larger screen and a proper keyboard are simply better tools for the job.

According to recent reports, but I'm not trying to replace my MacBook Pro. I'm trying to make the most of the powerful machine I already own, without needing to sit in front of it every time I want to accomplish something.

In a recent development, my iPad made coding remotely possible. The iPhone Duo has made it effortless.

The Duo's hardware makes this workflow convenient, but Workbench's thoughtful approach to the form factor, particularly its upcoming native terminal, is what makes the experience genuinely powerful.

Jensen Huang had a stunning fall from grace — from being one of the richest people on Earth and one of the primary drivers of the AI boom to being implicated in two extramarital affair scandals and resigning from Nvidia in under two weeks. While many are focused on the former Nvidia chief’s relationship with Alice Huang, who was allegedly passing on information to Chinese intelligence, the Wall Street Journal dug deeper into the person who introduced her to Jensen — Kang Wei, a star fund manager in Shanghai who also happened to be Ms. Huang’s husband.

There have been reports that Kang Wei met Jensen Huang in the 2010s, when his investment firm was heavily involved in Chinese gaming companies. It’s not clear if this introduction predated Kang’s relationship and marriage to Alice, but sources close to Ms. Huang said that she was able to get close to Jensen by the 2020s. Despite being a couple, the WSJ reported that Kang seemingly accepted Alice’s relationship with Jensen, with people close to the couple saying that he would often joke that she was a personal assistant to the billionaire.

Kang Wei is not just an average business executive, though. He made a name for himself in the finance world as a strategist for Shenyin Wanguo before taking over the Zhonghai Fund in 2007. This made him one of the youngest mutual fund chiefs in China at that time, before finally setting out on his own and founding Shanghai Hexi in 2010.

It was also around this time that Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le, entered the financial industry, first working at HSBC’s private banking arm in Hong Kong, before moving to CITIC Securities, where she attained a vice president position. It was during her time at CITIC that Alice crossed paths with Kang. Shanghai Hexi signed a deal with the securities firm in 2014 and 2015, and by 2016, corporate registry records show that Ms. Huang had joined the investment firm.

The Economic Times reports Alice Huang’s move into Shanghai Hexi resulted in her getting a 25% stake in the firm, all of which came from Kang. The remaining shares were shared between Kang Wei, with 48.75%, and his business partner, Zhu Xiaoming, with 26.25%, with Alice Huang’s 25% ownership stake being held through Shanghai Yuxi Investment Management Consulting Co., Ltd. Meanwhile, Kang also started introducing Alice Huang as his wife to his business associates and investors.

Sources indicate that one year later, Zhu and Kang had a falling out when one of their investments under a Hexi fund resulted in a major windfall, with the two partners disagreeing on how the profits were to be shared. Nevertheless, the massive profit generated by the deal allowed Shanghai Hexi to purchase Hangzhou Shengfeng, a video game company, for around 500 million yuan from Chinese conglomerate Century Huatong.

Recent findings suggest that two years after the transaction, in 2019, Hangzhou Shengfeng’s ownership was transferred to an offshore entity, which was eventually consolidated under Osmanthus Vale Holdings — a holding company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands and listed Huang Le, Alice Huang’s Chinese name, as its sole owner. It was then purchased by 7Road Holdings less than two months after it was founded. While Ms. Huang was the signatory in this deal, it’s believed that she served as a “white glove,” a person who operates on behalf of another to conceal their identity — but it remains unclear if this was for Shanghai Hexi and Kang Wei or some other third party.

Industry observers note that there is not much information on Alice Huang’s activities between 2019 and 2021. However, Shanghai Hexi invested in Shanghai Longjing Information Technology, a data center-focused subsidiary of Century Huatong in 2020, where Ms. Huang served as a director between 2021 and 2022, according to a report by The Wire China. At about the same time, 7Road Holdings expanded into cloud computing, just before ChatGPT brought AI LLMs to the forefront. The U.S. government’s ban on the export of Nvidia chips to China put this investment in jeopardy, though, forcing it to spin off the business as 7Road International in Singapore.

We don’t know when 7Road Holdings sold its Singapore subsidiary, but corporate records show that by the time the company was renamed Megaspeed in March 2023, it was already under the ownership of Huang Le Limited and led by Ms. Huang. It was sold again in November 2023 to Swiftdata, a company owned by Singaporean Tan Yong Pong. Axios remarked that she left the firm as a managing director soon after this acquisition, but sources said that she kept working with the company afterward, with Kang Wei helping her get it off the ground.

In the same year, Shanghai Century Litong was founded to build AI data centers in Shanghai and Shenzhen, with Jiangsu Lettall Electronic Co., an electronic components manufacturer, holding a 90% stake, while the remaining 10% is owned by Century Longteng, as reported by BigGo Finance. It should be noted that Century Longteng was renamed from Shanghai Yuxi Investment Management, with the firm pivoting its business from finance to cloud computing, and that even though Alice Huang has already exited the tech giant by this time, it’s under the control of Huang Yu, who some sources say is Ms. Huang’s sister.

A year after these data center acquisitions, Alice Huang began to be spotted in public with the former Nvidia CEO. A LinkedIn post showed her having drinks with a leather-clad Jensen Huang alongside other tech executives from NetThunder and Gigabyte at a post-Computex 2024 event. She was once again seen having dinner with him in a Taipei restaurant as reporters tried to interview him while one kid demanded his attention off camera.

But more than these public sightings, Alice herself boasted about her “closeness” to the then CEO. People close to her noted that she regularly posted photos with Jensen on her WeChat account, and even shared others with potential customers to help establish her credibility. She even reportedly claimed that Mr. Huang would celebrate her birthdays with restaurant dinners and gifts, with one Nvidia China sales employee also saying that she was a familiar face at the company’s annual event for China partners.

Recent findings suggest that an investigation revealed that from 2023 to 2025, Megaspeed imported $4.6 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips, while another $2 billion was routed through Speedmatrix, Megaspeed’s subsidiary with offices in Johor, Malaysia. Shanghai Century Litong also reportedly bought AI GPUs from other sources, with estimates putting the total number of banned chips moved through Alice Huang’s assistance at around 240,000, putting the shipments’ worth at around $7.5 billion.

It has been revealed that but even as Ms. Huang was making her international moves, Kang Wei was facing trouble at home. Chinese regulators fined him 2.5 million yuan, or approximately $380,000, in 2025, for violating sections of China’s Securities Law. This also led to a warning letter against him, issued in August 2026 by the China Securities Regulatory Commission. Despite running into trouble with the authorities, this massive paper trail highlighted how Kang Wei actively made moves that put Alice Huang close to Jensen Huang.

In a recent development, some questions remain, though, about the U.S. intelligence community’s claims that she worked with the Ministry of State Security (MSS), China’s primary intelligence and counterintelligence agency. If it’s true that Alice Huang worked with the MSS and passed on information to the agency, did she specifically target Jensen Huang, or did the spy agency simply discover their indiscretion and use that to force her to cooperate? Was all this planned by the MSS, or were they just shrewd business moves that allowed Kang to make more money while going under the radar of regulators? These are questions that only Kang Wei and Alice Huang (or the Chinese spy agency) can answer. But no matter the case, the fact remains that China acquired advanced AI chips that were supposed to be out of its reach because of this couple’s connections.

#352. Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth
