📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LangChain revealed on November 13, 2026 that it raised $300 million in a Series C round at a $3 billion valuation. Existing investor CapitalG led the financing.

In a recent development, the capital backs LangChain’s work on LangSmith, a platform for operating, improving and governing agents regardless of the framework used to build them. Its stated mission centers on letting enterprises choose their models, control data and infrastructure, improve agents continuously and apply governance for secure operation at scale.

According to recent reports, the round included significant participation from new investors GIC and DFJ Growth and existing investors IVP and Sapphire Ventures. Salesforce Ventures, Insight Venture Partners, QuantumLight and MongoDB Ventures also joined, while Sequoia, Amplify and Benchmark increased their participation.

LangChain expects agents built for specific domains to become standalone products and internal operational tools, differentiated by knowledge, data and user experience, with control of those systems forming the basis for lasting competitive advantage.

LangChain reports a LangSmith user base of more than 7,000 organizations. Its examples range from startups Harvey, Rippling and Listen Labs to Fortune 500 companies NVIDIA, Toyota and Salesforce. At Clay, the platform tracks hundreds of millions of agent runs each month and supports agent improvement. Workday uses LangSmith for organization-wide operation and governance, and cut the deployment time for a latest agent from five months to under a day.

Those deployments illustrate why LangChain groups monitoring and governance with deployment: a high-volume agent operation needs visibility after launch, while a large organization also needs a shorter, controlled path into production.

In a recent development, langSmith’s foundation is organized into Agent Runtime, Agent Improvement and Agent Governance. Agent Runtime covers the path from agent architecture to production infrastructure. Development teams use Deep Agents, LangGraph and LangChain to retain model choice and decide how context is managed. Secure, scaled deployment runs through LangSmith Agent Server and Sandboxes in either cloud or customer environments, while LangSmith Managed Agents and Fleet offer a fully managed route to production.

Agent Improvement pairs measurement with automated remediation. LangSmith Observability and Evaluation expose agent behavior and assess quality. LangChain says LangSmith Engine, its in-platform agent, looks for errors, produces code and prompt corrections, and checks production traffic for regressions. LangSmith Fine-Tuning helps teams convert agent traces into training data that can be used to tune and evaluate specialized models.

The governance pillar centralizes control of models, tools and data. Teams can use the LLM and Tool Gateways to set model budgets and fallback behavior, safeguard sensitive information, and manage tool access and authentication across teams and agents.

LangChain has scheduled a release event for November 20, 2026, where it plans to share several additional LangSmith capabilities built on this foundation.

The central question for those releases is whether they make high-performing agents easier to build while preserving customers’ control over models, data, infrastructure and governance.

In a recent development, the Tribit FlyBuds C3 are a good set of wireless earbuds, with impressive sound quality for the money, strong EQ options, and a comfortable fit. However, their underwhelming battery life and plasticky build slightly hold them back. And while they’re temptingly cheap, their limited ANC is the one thing that stops me from recommending them over similarly priced rivals.

Good sound quality with powerful bass.

It has been revealed that why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.

In a recent development, these aren’t just any earbuds, they’re FlyBuds. And the latest Tribit FlyBuds 3 look mighty impressive at a glance, especially when you consider their temptingly low price tag.

Sources indicate that the Tribit FlyBuds 3 bring active noise cancellation, highly customizable EQ, and a six-microphone system for 'clear' voice calls. Sounds pretty good for $39.99 / £49.99 (about AU$60), right? But just how good are the FlyBuds C3? I’ve been using them for a couple of weeks now, and this is my verdict.

First up, let’s talk about features. The Tribit FlyBuds C3 offer a lot of the functionality you’d expect from the best wireless earbuds.

Perhaps the main thing is ANC, which has five levels of strength, and can apparently block sounds “up to 45dB”. I have to say, though, that ANC on the FlyBuds C3 is disappointing. On walks, the sounds of nearby chatter and vehicles passing by were dulled, but still pretty audible. And when working in the office, the noise of typing was still pretty clear, even with my music at about 70% volume.

Recent findings suggest that again, the ANC here will certainly dull your surroundings, but it won’t block them out entirely. With that said, there is a very effective ambient mode that helps you stay aware of your environment when listening to tunes or taking phone calls on the go.

Recent findings suggest that most of the other features here did impress me, though. You get pretty detailed EQ options, with a number of presets for specific genres and use cases, as well as a full 10-band equalizer if you’re looking for more granular control. In addition, there’s a low-latency game mode, multi-point connectivity, and a hearing protection option.

Something else I appreciated about the FlyBuds C3 was their inclusion of customizable touch controls. By disabling single touch commands, and mapping playback controls to double taps (as well as ANC alterations to press and hold), I was able to avoid accidentally triggering unwanted button presses. You can map specific controls to each individual bud too, which is a great touch.

Sources indicate that I also found the mic quality here to be plenty good enough. When taking phone calls and making a recording, I found that my speech was replicated accurately — I didn’t have to put up with the almost ‘underwater’ quality that some cheap models can apply. I picked up a bit of sibilance, and the microphones’ ability to carve out background noise was pretty limited, but in my view the call quality here is adequate for the price.

There are a few areas that could be improved, though. The X-3D spatial mode just makes music sound louder and less refined, there’s no wear detection or higher-res audio codec support, and the battery life here is surprisingly average.

Yes, you get just five hours from the buds with ANC active and seven hours without noise cancelling on, with up to 35 hours of playtime available with the case (with ANC off). A lot of Tribit’s budget audio tech goes substantial on battery, so I was expecting more here — that five hours with ANC on is especially weak when you consider you’ll need to use the standard EQ and keep volume at 50% or less to achieve it.

The FlyBuds C3 have been a bit of a mixed bag so far, but how do they fare when it comes to sound quality?

Let’s make a few things clear, though. These earbuds aren’t going to provide a wide, nuanced soundstage, impeccable detailing, or expert instrument separation. They can’t provide the quality that a pair of wired earbuds in this price-range, like the Sennheiser CX 80U can open up, for example, and keep things pretty basic. But you know what, they actually get those basics pretty spot on.

They definitely emphasize the bass first, but this works to good effect. When tuning into Right Before My Eyes by N'n'G, the pounding low end hit with impressive depth and agility, without sounding muddy or unregimented. Vocals in the midrange weren’t particularly open or detailed, but they were relatively clear, and drums in the treble was articulate and snappy.

When listening to the 2020 remaster of Giant Steps by John Coltrane, I felt that instruments in the midrange sounded a touch recessed, but by giving them a bump with some EQ tweaks, they sounded clean and fairly expressive, and the keys were well-separated from the leading sax.

Overall, the FlyBuds C3 provide good sound for their price. Treble can get a little edgy at the higher volumes, and the mid-range needs a bit of tweaking to sound its best, but the powerful bass really shines here.

In a recent development, in terms of design, the FlyBuds C3 keep it pretty simple, and that’s no bad thing. The earbuds themselves are small and lightweight, and are housed in a curved, ultra-compact charging case, making them perfect for sliding into your pocket. While the buds do have a plasticky and cheap-looking appearance, this can be forgiven for the price, and they do look curved and fairly stylish in-use, whether you go for the black or white color variant.

According to recent reports, you also get small, medium, and large ear tips in the box, enabling you to find the perfect fit. For me, the medium ear tips were spot on, and I found the C3 to be very comfortable in use, with no signs of fatigue after a full day’s use. IP55 waterproofing also makes these safe to use when working out or listening in light rain.

The Tribit FlyBuds C3 sound pretty solid for the price, offer decent comfort, and have pretty generous EQ options. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that air travelers in the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that thankfully, this did not affect other safety services, like Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS), which primarily relied on hardware in aircraft that communicated with other transponders to help prevent accidents.
  • It has been revealed that the problem first became apparent at Indianapolis Center, which monitors the airspace in northern Kentucky, southern Indiana, southern Ohio, and parts of West Virginia, when the personnel working at the site had trouble communicating with flight crews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that air travelers in the U.S. were in for a nasty surprise last Friday night after the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) called for a nationwide ground stop. According to the Wall Street Journal, the issue started after a newly installed Juniper router, built by HP Enterprise, started broadcasting to a wide part of the network. This, in turn, overloaded the established and antiquated system, resulting in communications glitches and interruptions between air traffic control and pilots.

Recent findings suggest that thankfully, this did not affect other safety services, like Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS), which primarily relied on hardware in aircraft that communicated with other transponders to help prevent accidents. Still, air traffic’s inability to communicate with high-flying aircraft made it impossible to coordinate the thousands of airborne aircraft at any given time, forcing the agency to call for an emergency ground stop. A nationwide ground stop order is quite a drastic move, and it has only been invoked twice before. The first such event was on September 11, 2001, when terrorists infamously used hijacked airliners as weapons. The second was on January 11, 2023, when the agency’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, which sends warnings to pilots and air crews of crucial information crucial to flight safety, suffered from an outage for about a couple of hours.

It has been revealed that the problem first became apparent at Indianapolis Center, which monitors the airspace in northern Kentucky, southern Indiana, southern Ohio, and parts of West Virginia, when the personnel working at the site had trouble communicating with flight crews. The agency then went on a nationwide hunt for the glitch, and it soon found two possible sources — an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Upon deeper inspection, the agency discovered that new routers recently installed in both places have begun sending out a high volume of data across the entire FAA communications network.

Sources indicate that “We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds,” FAA technology chief Rebecca Guy said in a press conference. This might seem like a minor hiccup for any modern network, which could typically handle connections in the hundreds of thousands, or even millions, per second. For example, one of the largest recorded DDoS attacks for 2026 saw traffic spike to 31.4 TB/s, which is enough to takedown an entire country’s web infrastructure.

However, the FAA still uses an antiquated copper network, which was easily overwhelmed by the amount of data that the routers sent. This network is already several decades old, so the agency is at the moment in the process of upgrading everything to fiber, which is costing taxpayers billions of dollars. Even as the agency is in this period of transition, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has raised several questions. “Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration? Or was it just a bad piece of router technology that we put into this system that propagated these errors?” Bedford said in statement on Saturday. He also added that the agency is investigating the incident. As for the Juniper router, an HPE spokesperson said that they appear to be working as intended and that “They did not fail.” It was eventually discovered that a specific feature on the router caused the system overload, with FAA employees turning it off across the entire network on all Juniper routers.

It took about four hours for the FAA to return its communications network to normal, but repercussions go way beyond that. Passengers aboard all those canceled and diverted flights needed to be served, even as new passengers kept on arriving for their scheduled flights. It’s been estimated that airlines needed a few days to recover after the CrowdStrike crash of 2024 forced United, Delta, and American Airlines to cancel flights (except for Southwest, which avoided the chaos because it used an antiquated OS from the 1990s), so we expect passengers unlucky enough to be in transit during this incident to suffer waits between a few hours to a day or two before their journeys could continue.

#209. Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing

Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing.
  • Nov 12, 2026 3 min read.
  • According to recent reports, technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing.

Nov 12, 2026 3 min read.

According to recent reports, technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering. It can be the price of learning through software in use. As AI accelerates code production beyond our capacity to understand code and context, technical debt increasingly becomes a sociotechnical challenge, Xin Yao noted in her talk "What If Your Biggest Technical Debt Is Social", at GOTO Copenhagen.

Yao quoted Ward Cunningham, who defined debt as "not-quite-right code". Debt sounds like a negative thing, but it can be a deliberate business strategy, she explained:.

If we release the code now, well knowing it’s not perfect for the future yet, we’ll get some business feedback, we’ll get some user feedback, we’ll probably get paid for something, and that’s good as a business strategy.

Debt isn’t about poorly written code; it arises when we design software with incomplete knowledge. Hence, debt is the price of learning by doing, Yao argued. Releasing software allows us to test our assumptions against reality. Once we’ve got a learning experience, we have to put that experience back into our code and pay off the debt, she added. The debt becomes problematic when our software doesn’t catch up with our latest learning.

In a recent development, debt can be a good communication strategy toward management. It provides an economic argument for the cost of postponing architectural improvements. However, framing technical debt solely as something to eliminate misses its strategic value. The question is not whether to incur debt, but whether the learning it enables justifies the cost, and whether we actually repay it.

Yao referred to Kent Beck’s article "Earn and Learn," which explores features vs. futures. Features deliver value today, while the future is actually the optionality to adapt those features, Yao explained:.

According to recent reports, every bit of code already coded is complexity and a constraint. Every feature removes some future. If you go on producing features, maybe using your LLMs, then at a certain point, all you can do is use your capacity to pay the interest, to fix the code, and you can no longer release features.

Industry observers note that the challenge is to balance delivering features with preserving future options, Yao stated. Sometimes, delaying a design commitment preserves options until we know more, and this includes postponing some upfront architecture decisions to the last responsible moment as well. As Beck argues, waiting is not laziness; waiting is holding an asset.

According to recent reports, technical debt can therefore be understood as learning made visible in software. We design based on what we know, observe software’s impact, modularity, and its architecture’s implications, and we patch our understanding, Yao explained:.

The software no longer fits what we now understand, and yesterday’s good understanding becomes today’s debt.

AI introduces a fresh challenge: software can now be produced faster than teams can develop a shared understanding of its behavior, design decisions and consequences, Yao argued.

It has been revealed that agentic coding makes debt repayment more complex; beyond addressing poorly written AI-generated code, teams must close the gap between what the software actually does and what they understand it to do, while ensuring the code keeps pace with their evolving domain and architectural understanding. Paying off debt is no longer just a technical task, but a sociotechnical one, Yao concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Xin Yao after her talk.

InfoQ: What does learning from technical debt look like, and what benefit does it bring?

Xin Yao: We design and release software based on our best current understanding, then test our assumptions against business and user reality. Paying off debt means incorporating that learning back into the software and closing the gap between what we knew when we released the first iteration and what we know now.

Each iteration creates new debt and new learning. Small batches and tight feedback loops help teams retain the memory of their initial design decisions and continuously repay the old debt with new learning.

InfoQ: What does technical debt look like now that developers are using artificial intelligence?

Sources indicate that yao: With agentic coding, software production can outpace human understanding. Code increasingly becomes a fossil record of agents’ decisions, while humans remain accountable for its consequences. Local productivity gains can create collective costs: more code, weaker ownership and growing gaps in shared understanding.

A study on How Developers Discuss the Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development describes this as "a tragedy of the commons". The danger is not merely more poorly written agentic code, but accelerated learning debt across the sociotechnical system.

Victor Coimbra is CTO and Managing Partner at Artefact, where he leads AI, data science, and engineering work across the Americas. His career combines business strategy experience at Bain and Accenture with hands-on leadership delivering AI and machine learning systems in complex enterprise environments. He focuses on helping organizations connect technical capabilities with measurable business outcomes, including the architecture, governance, and operating models needed to scale AI.

Artefact is a global data and AI consulting company that helps enterprises develop strategies, build data platforms, deploy AI solutions, and manage organizational change. Its work spans industries including financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, and retail. Ahead of its Adopt AI Summit, taking place December 3–4, 2026, at the Grand Palais in Paris, Coimbra discusses how enterprises can move beyond pilots, build teams that combine people and AI agents, and measure the value of AI in production.

Your career has taken you from business strategy at Accenture to leading AI, data science, and engineering teams at Artefact across the Americas. How has this combination of strategic consulting and hands-on technical leadership shaped your approach to helping enterprises turn AI investments into measurable business outcomes?

It has been revealed that it taught me to always connect AI strategy to delivery. Strategy at Bain and Accenture revealed me that executives buy a change in a P&L line. Engineering taught me that a lot of that value can get lost between the slide and production.

Today AI is less about technology and more about building a moat around your core business operations. The key question is how to turn individual productivity into collective enterprise value, with a true shared cognitive capacity across the company.

That takes a mix of strategy and delivery, and it is something I learned a lot from doing both.

In a recent development, despite significant investment in artificial intelligence, many organizations still struggle to move beyond successful pilot projects. In your experience, what are the most common obstacles preventing enterprise AI initiatives from reaching production, and what distinguishes companies that successfully scale their deployments?

It has been revealed that in my experience, many pilots stall because AI is added to an organization that was designed for humans only. The technology usually works. What is often still open is the division of work: which tasks belong to agents, which stay with humans, who reviews, and who owns the result.

On top of that, 3 needs tend to slow the scale-up: token costs that explode with usage-based pricing, security and governance, and adoption that never turns access into real usage.

According to recent reports, the companies I see scaling well treat AI as an organizational redesign. They split delivery into 2 loops. In the inner loop, agents execute end to end: code, build, test, push, review. In the outer loop, humans set the intent, verify the result and monitor cost and quality. Then they build one platform underneath and reuse it for every use case.

You’ve written about the importance of building an AI-native organization rather than simply adding chatbots and copilots to existing systems. What fundamental changes to enterprise technology architecture are necessary to support this transition, and where are businesses right now underinvesting?

Industry observers note that an AI-native organization runs on a platform, and that platform is the sum of 4 layers: Harness, Context, Model and Infra. The Harness is where humans and agents meet and work, the full application around the model. Context defines what agents know and what authority they have. Model is how models are accessed, routed and governed at the right cost. Infra is where they actually run, and who holds the keys.

Naturally, most of the attention goes to the visible 20%: copilots and chat tools. The hidden 80% is where most of the engineering lives, and where cost, security and control are decided.

Recent findings suggest that my suggestion is simple. Buy generalist harnesses and build the industry-specific ones. Rent and experiment on models and infra, because they change every quarter. And own your context completely. It is the layer that is truly yours, and where I see the biggest opportunity to invest more.

According to recent reports, as AI evolves from assisting employees to autonomously executing complex workflows, how should organizations determine which processes are appropriate for agentic automation? What technical and operational safeguards must be established before granting AI agents greater decision-making authority?

Recent findings suggest that the way I see it, agents are very good at work that looks to the past, humans at work that looks to the future. Agents excel at anything built on existing information, like analytics, coding, testing, documentation and reconciliation. Humans own what needs creativity, and creativity by definition looks forward: taste, vision, planning, deciding, and judging whether a result is actually good.

In practice that maps to the 2 loops. Agents run the inner loop and execute. Humans keep the outer loop: intent, verification and monitoring.

Industry observers note that the safeguards are engineered, not prompted. We use 6 harness layers: task capture, memory, a secure workbench with sandboxed runtime and permissions, a loop with checkpoints and clarifications, model routing, and guardrails that define what an agent cannot do alone, like human approvals, policy checks and PII controls. Autonomy then grows with the track record, the same way it does for a upcoming hire.

You’ve described AI agents as teammates rather than conventional software tools. How does this perspective change the way organizations should structure teams, assign responsibilities, and train employees to collaborate with increasingly autonomous AI systems?

It has been revealed that we are already in the hybrid organization. The question I find most important now is how to divide the workforce between humans and agents. I believe it is the key to scaling.

Industry observers note that in a hybrid team, the org chart allocates cognitive capacity, not headcount. A typical split I see in a mature tech team is 15% human-only work, 25% augmented work and 60% done by agents. The Head of IT sets intent, allocates capacity and owns outcome and cost. A senior developer verifies agent deliveries and decides architecture. An orchestrator agent routes tasks and reports cost, and a review agent checks every delivery.

Recent findings suggest that the gains compound in 3 steps. Augmented employees deliver around 5x. Agents as synthetic employees doing end-to-end work deliver around 10x. Orchestrating both as one workforce is where I believe the 1000x potential lies.

Industry observers note that training follows the same logic. People learn to brief an agent like a junior engineer, with structured context and clear outcomes, and to spend their time on taste, planning and decisions.

Industry observers note that enterprise AI systems depend heavily on reliable data infrastructure, yet many organizations continue to struggle with fragmented data, inconsistent governance, and legacy technology. What foundational capabilities should businesses prioritize when preparing their data platforms for agentic AI, and how can they modernize without disrupting existing operations?

It has been revealed that design your data platform for a new kind of consumer: agents. A dashboard with a wrong number gets questioned by a human. An agent with a wrong number acts on it, at scale.

Recent findings suggest that prioritize 4 capabilities. Shared business definitions, so every agent and team means the same thing by “active customer.” An integration gateway with authentication and standard protocols like MCP, so agents access data with the permissions of the role they act for. Observable quality and lineage. And unstructured data treated as a first-class asset, because contracts, tickets and meeting notes hold most of the real knowledge.

It has been revealed that to modernize without disruption, wrap legacy systems first and migrate use case by use case. Agents also change the economics here. Multi-agent migration pipelines now modernize hundreds of thousands of lines of legacy code in months, with humans deciding the architecture.

Beyond access to structured data, AI agents increasingly require an understanding of institutional knowledge, business processes, and organizational context. How can enterprises effectively capture and integrate this knowledge into their AI systems, and what risks arise when agents operate without sufficient business context?

Context is what turns a model into a colleague. Tools understand tasks, agents understand context. You don’t ask a junior engineer to work without explaining the goal, the constraints and what good looks like, and an agent is no different.

Capture knowledge from the work itself, rather than from large documentation projects that are hard to keep up to date. Every meeting, ticket, decision and correction feeds a context layer that combines files, tables, vectors and a graph of relationships. Every finished task writes back to memory, so the organization learns with each delivery. And context needs its own governance: evals, permissions and cost control.

Without context, agents tend to struggle in a few predictable ways. They follow the written rule and miss the unwritten one everyone knows. They retrieve the wrong information and answer with total confidence. They work on last quarter’s facts. And a context layer without strict permissions can put sensitive data at risk.

Many companies measure AI success through productivity improvements, adoption rates, or the number of pilots rolled out. What metrics should CIOs and business leaders use to evaluate genuine AI return on investment, particularly when accounting for infrastructure costs, ongoing maintenance, and the operational complexity of autonomous agents?

Measure the hybrid workforce, not the tool. Adoption is only the first of 4 levels, always against a baseline taken before rollout. Adoption asks if people use it. Productivity asks if we deliver faster: lead time, throughput, resolution time. Quality asks if the output is better: escaped defects, change failure rate, rework. Value and cost ask if it is worth it: effort freed, time to market, full cost per task.

Industry observers note that one metric that is easy to overlook is how cognitive capacity moves between humans and agents, team by team. Freed human capacity has to be redeployed to future-facing work with intent. Otherwise part of the gain gets lost.

Recent findings suggest that on cost, pricing is moving from flat fees to usage, which can make bills harder to predict, so model routing and FinOps belong in the platform from day 1. Treat AI spend like cloud spend: visible, attributed to a team, and tied to value.

It has been revealed that artefact works with enterprises across financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, retail, and other industries where AI adoption presents different challenges. What lessons are emerging from real-world deployments in these sectors, and how should organizations balance innovation with regulatory compliance, reliability, and human oversight?

It has been revealed that every sector faces the same question: how to divide the work between humans and agents. What changes is how much of the outer loop must stay human. In retail and consumer goods, mistakes are cheap, so agents take more of the work faster. In manufacturing, reliability and integration with operational systems set the pace. In financial services and healthcare, every decision must be explainable, so humans keep more of verification and decision for longer.

It has been revealed that the lesson I see everywhere is that compliance works best as a property of the platform, built in from the start. When guardrails, audit logs and human approvals live in the harness, every new use case inherits them. When compliance comes only at the end, each new project has to start that conversation again.

Oversight should be tiered. Agents act alone on low-risk tasks, get reviewed by exception on medium risk, and only prepare the decision on high risk. The tiers move as trust is earned.

With Artefact’s Adopt AI Summit taking place in Paris this December, discussions around AI sovereignty, governance, and industrial competitiveness are becoming increasingly important. How do you see Europe’s approach to AI adoption influencing global enterprise strategies, and what developments do you believe will define the next phase of enterprise AI over the coming years?

Europe was early in asking the sovereignty question, and I think it is becoming a global design principle. Multinationals don’t want one architecture per regulation, so they design for the strictest one: own your context, rent your models, and keep control of where they run and who holds the keys. The next opportunity for Europe is to bring the same energy to adoption, because competitiveness will come from usage at scale.

The next phase is the hybrid organization, and I believe it is the future of work. Companies will move from counting headcount to managing a shared cognitive capacity between humans and agents. Agents will take most of the work that looks to the past: analysis, code, reporting. Humans will move to the work that looks to the future: taste, vision, planning and decisions.

Industry observers note that I believe the companies that solve the division of work first will lead the way. That is the conversation I want to have in Paris to define the next years.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to learn more about enterprise AI adoption, agentic workflows, and data transformation should visit Artefact.

Antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

Industry observers note that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

  • Last year, Jensen Huang sold up to six million Nvidia shares, netting him around $925 million.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that nvidia Board Director Mark Stevens sold about 4.2 million of his shares, netting him around $1 billion in cash, almost exactly two months before Jensen Huang was accused of having “close ties” to an alleged Chinese spy. According to Moneywise.com, Stevens started the sale from August 31 to September 2, when Nvidia stock hovered between $220 and $226, which made him $411 million. The next tranche, totaling $236 million, came in the next couple of days as Nvidia traded from $227 to $234. The final sale happened on September 18 at around $220 per share, making Stevens approximately $300 million. These three transactions would have made him somewhere around $947 million.

Last year, Jensen Huang sold up to six million Nvidia shares, netting him around $925 million. However, unlike Stevens, who had no plan, this move was declared six months earlier in a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan to help avoid accusations of insider trading.

Sources indicate that nvidia’s stock price has taken a beating since the scandal broke, with the company trading at $162.85 at the time of writing, its lowest level in the past 12 months. When the story first broke at the end of October, Nvidia shares were at around $205. It then started sliding, with the price at $178.67 after Jensen admitted to the affair last Sunday, although he did not name the involved party.

A second affair was revealed a few days after the former Nvidia chief’s confession, leading to his resignation from the tech giant a few hours after that. The news sent Nvidia stock down to $151.09 — a nearly 25% drop from before the scandal. It recovered somewhat after the initial shock, climbing to nearly $170 before Friday’s trading, but took a beating again soon after the market opened.

According to recent reports, despite the sale, Stevens still holds about 27.5 million Nvidia shares, making him the second-largest shareholder after Jensen and Lori Huang. The price difference between today and September 18 is around $57, meaning he would have lost 25% of the value if he had sold after the scandal broke. Furthermore, his remaining Nvidia shares have lost more than $1.5 billion in value in just one quarter. Still, selling one’s holdings in a company as a board director does not constitute a crime. After all, it's unlikely that one could have predicted how hard Jensen Huang would fall in such a short time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CXMT is reportedly building 10 latest chip fabs and is stated to be able of flooding the market with chips by 2028, helping to decrease chips prices.

According to recent reports, CXMT, one of China’s bigger chips manufacturers, is reportedly looking at building more chip fabs that would allow it to direct more memory chips onto the market. Doing so would make more product available, and that could help prices come down on at least one component that has cause the prices of products to skyrocket across the consumer electronics industry.

Right now, memory chips are at all-time high prices for manufacturers, and that cost has been passed onto the consumer via increased prices of RAM sticks, smartphones, laptops, game consoles like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch 2, and just about anything that has memory in it. Even NVIDIA’s seven-year old NVIDIA SHIELD TV Pro has gone up in price to $299. But speculation from new reports suggest that CXMT could help change all that, and sooner than people think.

It has been revealed that according to reporting from TechNews, via TrendForce and spotted by Abhishek Yadav on X, CXMT is mentioned to be already in the process of building up to ten more chip fabs and looking to flood the market with memory chips by 2028. This is according to “Charles Kau,” who is referred to as the “Godfather of DRAM,” the reports say.

With chips flooding the market, this is suspected to cause prices to come down on other memory from brands like Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. It’s also stated, however, that CXMT’s chips aren’t expected to match the quality of those three companies, but that CXMT would still proposal to flood the market.

While the company is expected to be building 10 new fabs and starting production on chips, Kau has reportedly stated that CXMT won’t be making DRAM memory, just the chips used in the production of it.

#203. Tech Report: Dropbox Shares How Its In-House Cookie Auditor Tests Consent Behaviour Across 200+ Web Surfaces

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Infoq

Tech Report: Dropbox Shares How Its In-House Cookie Auditor Tests Consent Behaviour Across 200+ Web Surfaces

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (329 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nov 13, 2026 2 min read.
  • Sources indicate that dropbox built what it calls "an auditor for our auditor," a companion URL detector that uses traffic data to find every live Dropbox web surface.
  • Platform engineers interested in building similar tooling can see the shape of a minimal Playwright assertion in a recent qaskills.sh guide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nov 13, 2026 2 min read.

Sources indicate that dropbox built what it calls "an auditor for our auditor," a companion URL detector that uses traffic data to find every live Dropbox web surface. Billions of visit records are filtered down to a manageable list of unique paths, then grouped by consent logic so that representative URLs can stand in for large families of similar pages.

Platform engineers interested in building similar tooling can see the shape of a minimal Playwright assertion in a recent qaskills.sh guide.

Today the auditor produces a weekly report for Privacy and Engineering teams, separating likely violations from known false positives and tracking historical trends. Dropbox's next planned iteration is routing findings directly to the teams that own each page, shortening the loop between detection and fix. The team notes that the browser automation itself may be the simplest part of such a project, with the harder work sitting around it: defining correct behaviour, maintaining an accurate inventory and separating real issues from noise.

Dropbox is a cloud-based file hosting and collaboration platform founded in 2007 by Drew Houston and Arash Ferdowsi and headquartered in San Francisco. The company operates more than 200 web surfaces across its product lineup, which includes Dropbox, Dropbox Sign, DocSend and FormSwift, and has invested heavily in privacy and compliance programmes covering GDPR, CCPA and ISO 27018.

Playwright is an open-source browser automation library developed and maintained by Microsoft. It drives Chromium, WebKit and Firefox through a single API across JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java and .NET, and has become a widely used tool for end-to-end testing, web scraping and, increasingly, automated privacy and compliance audits of the kind Dropbox describes.
